questions.stem: Which political change does the specification name as a cause of globalisation?
options: The breakdown of the Soviet system and the opening up of China
The formation of the World Trade Organization
The introduction of the euro
The creation of the United Nations
questions.why: Together they brought hundreds of millions of workers and consumers into the world market economy within a generation.
whyNot: The WTO relates to trade liberalisation, a separate named cause.
The euro relates to monetary union within a bloc.
The UN is not named as a cause.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines trade liberalisation?
options: The reduction or removal of barriers to international trade
The privatisation of state-owned exporters
The floating of a country's exchange rate
The signing of an agreement to fix commodity prices
questions.why: It has occurred through multilateral negotiation and through a growing number of regional and bilateral agreements.
whyNot: That is privatisation.
That is exchange rate policy.
That is a commodity agreement.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines technology transfer?
options: The spread of technology, methods and know-how from a foreign investor to local firms and workers
The export of high-technology goods
The purchase of patents by a government
The relocation of a research laboratory
questions.why: It is one of the main potential benefits of FDI for a recipient country, and it depends on local capacity to absorb it.
whyNot: That is a trade flow.
That is one narrow mechanism, not the definition.
That is a location decision.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a reason a firm undertakes FDI?
options: To produce inside a tariff wall and avoid trade barriers
To reduce the total size of its operations
To avoid having to employ any workers
To reduce its exposure to all forms of risk
questions.why: Market access, lower costs, resources, avoiding barriers and acquiring brands are the standard reasons.
whyNot: FDI expands operations.
FDI involves employing workers in the host country.
FDI adds political and exchange rate risk.

questions.stem: Why is it argued that falling communication costs mattered more than falling tariffs?
options: Cheap coordination made global supply chains possible, not just global selling
Communication costs fell by a larger percentage
Tariffs have never fallen significantly
Communication is unaffected by government policy
questions.why: Without cheap coordination a firm could export but could not manage production it did not stand beside. It also made services tradable.
whyNot: The size of the fall is not the argument.
Average tariffs have fallen substantially over decades.
Policy does affect telecommunications, but that is not the point.

questions.stem: How do trading blocs both cause and work against globalisation?
options: They create trade between members and divert it away from more efficient non-members
They raise tariffs between members and lower them for non-members
They prevent all trade with countries outside the bloc
They have no effect on trade patterns
questions.why: Naming that tension is worth a mark, because blocs are simultaneously a cause of integration and a form of discrimination.
whyNot: It is the other way round: internal barriers fall and an external tariff applies.
Trade with non-members continues, subject to the external tariff.
They substantially change the geographic pattern of trade.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a benefit of FDI to a recipient country?
options: It fills the savings gap and brings technology and skills
It guarantees a permanent balance of payments surplus
It eliminates the need for domestic investment
It removes the need for any taxation
questions.why: It also creates employment, raises growth and widens the tax base, subject to the costs.
whyNot: Profit repatriation makes the long-run effect on the current account negative.
Domestic investment remains essential.
Taxation is still required, and tax holidays reduce the revenue benefit.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cost of FDI to a recipient country?
options: Profit repatriation is a permanent outflow, and the investment may be footloose
It reduces the country's total output
It prevents the country from exporting
It always lowers wages below the local average
questions.why: Tax holidays and transfer pricing also reduce the revenue benefit, and local competitors may be crowded out.
whyNot: FDI normally raises output.
It often raises exports from the host country.
Multinationals typically pay above the local average, though below their home rate.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of containerisation?
options: It standardised handling, so loading a ship took hours rather than days
It reduced the size of ships and therefore their fuel use
It allowed governments to inspect every shipment
It made air freight unnecessary
questions.why: Larger vessels then lowered cost per unit shipped further, and air freight made high-value and perishable goods tradable.
whyNot: Vessels became much larger, not smaller.
Containerisation reduced the practicality of inspecting every shipment.
Air freight grew alongside it for different goods.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the strongest evidence that globalisation is a trend rather than a one-way process?
options: Tariffs have been reimposed, investment screened and supply chains deliberately shortened
Trade has never grown faster than output
FDI has never exceeded portfolio investment
Communication costs have started to rise
questions.why: Globalisation is driven by policy and technology, and policy can reverse.
whyNot: Trade grew faster than output for several decades.
FDI grew faster than trade for long periods.
Communication costs have continued to fall.

questions.stem: Why does technology transfer from FDI often disappoint?
options: The most valuable research stays in the home country and local absorption depends on education
Technology cannot legally cross borders
Host governments prohibit it
Multinationals have no technology to transfer
questions.why: Transfer requires local firms and workers capable of using the technology, which depends on the education system.
whyNot: Technology moves readily; the question is whether it is shared.
Most host governments actively seek it.
They typically hold substantial technology.

questions.stem: Which asymmetry should shape the conclusion of an essay on FDI?
options: Benefits are immediate and visible; several costs are gradual and cumulative
Benefits are gradual; costs are immediate
Both benefits and costs appear immediately
Neither benefits nor costs can be measured
questions.why: Jobs and investment appear at once, while profit repatriation and environmental damage accumulate, which is why governments compete for FDI and are later disappointed.
whyNot: Jobs and the investment itself appear immediately.
Repatriation and environmental effects build over years.
Both are partially measurable.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines footloose capital?
options: Investment with no strong tie to a location, which can be relocated relatively easily
Investment financed entirely by borrowing
Investment in transport infrastructure
Investment made by a government rather than a firm
questions.why: It is why incentives buy investment that may not stay once they expire.
whyNot: The financing method is not the issue.
Transport investment is usually immobile.
Ownership does not determine mobility.

questions.stem: Why did the opening of large economies affect global wages?
options: It roughly doubled the labour available to internationally mobile capital
It reduced the total world labour force
It raised wages equally in every country
It had no effect on labour markets
questions.why: That held down wages for lower-skilled work in developed economies and raised them where the work moved.
whyNot: It substantially increased the effective labour supply.
The effects ran in opposite directions in different places.
The wage effects are among the most studied consequences.

questions.stem: What determines how much of an FDI project's value stays in the host country?
options: Local sourcing, local employment at all levels, reinvested profit and tax actually paid
The size of the investing company's global revenue
The number of countries the investor operates in
The exchange rate on the day of the investment
questions.why: An operation importing all its inputs and repatriating its profit creates jobs and little else.
whyNot: Global scale says nothing about local retention.
Geographic spread is not the relevant measure.
A single day's rate is not structural.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a named cause of globalisation in the last fifty years?
options: An increase in the number and size of trading blocs
A rise in world population growth rates
A fall in global inequality between countries
The invention of the internal combustion engine
questions.why: The five named causes are trade liberalisation, more and larger blocs, political change, cheaper transport and communications, and the growing significance of TNCs.
whyNot: Population growth is not a named cause.
That is an effect rather than a cause.
It long predates the period specified.
